sources.note: Assigns credit in coding-agent RL by splitting each code diff into sub-diffs, matching semantically similar sub-diffs across rollouts to form advantage groups, and projecting the resulting diff-level advantage back onto the tokens that produced it.
sources.title: DiDPO: Diff-in-Diff Policy Optimization for Coding Agent Training

sources.note: Replaces GRPO's z-score group normalisation with a temperature-scaled softmax over rewards, which keeps the induced prompt-difficulty weighting bounded as pass probability approaches one and turns the temperature into a dial between REINFORCE and maximum-likelihood weighting.
sources.title: SoftmaxGRPO: Learning to Reason using Softmax Advantage Group Estimation

sources.note: Explores in weight space rather than token space during RLVR by sampling policies from a variational posterior at rollout time, and introduces a training-time exploration metric -- how often a method produces a correct rollout on a prompt where GRPO produced none -- because entropy and pass@k cannot tell exploration from degeneration.
sources.title: Parameter Exploration for RLVR via Variational Learning

sources.note: Gives the teacher branch of an on-policy self-distillation setup an abstract skill card -- a principle, when it applies, and the mistakes to avoid -- instead of the reference solution, so the privileged signal carries no answer and the gain lands on exactly the rollout groups where group-relative reward is algebraically silent.
sources.title: Distill Skills into Weights, Not Prompts: Abstract Skills as Privileged Signals for On-Policy Self-Distillation

sources.note: Fine-tunes a 1.7B model to read structured summaries of a time series and allocate ensemble weights across candidate forecasters, trained by SFT on rule-generated chains of thought and then by GRPO with a bounded reciprocal reward that keeps a continuous error gap from collapsing the group advantage.
sources.title: REATS: LLM Reasoning-based Ensemble Learning for Adaptive Time Series Forecasting

sources.note: Trains open-ended medical question answering by scoring each response against rubric criteria that three frontier models independently agreed on, grading each criterion as correct, missing or wrong rather than yes/no, and recovering a gradient in groups where every response ties by judging the responses pairwise in both orders.
sources.title: ConRub-Med: Reinforcement Learning with Consensus Rubrics for Open-Ended Medical Question Answering

sources.note: Points out that the group-relative policy gradient is a second-order U-statistic over pairs of rollouts rather than a sum of independent per-rollout contributions, and reallocates rollout compute accordingly -- treating prefixes as vertices and pair-gradient terms as edges, then correcting the resulting selection bias by inverse joint-inclusion weighting.
sources.title: PAIR: Pairwise-Aware Inclusion Reweighting for Adaptive Rollout Allocation in RLVR

result.definition: A prompt whose sampled rollouts all receive the same reward, so the group-relative advantage is exactly zero and the rollouts contribute no gradient -- the characteristic waste of critic-free reinforcement learning, since the compute was spent and the learning signal is nil. Across 7 sources it is measured rather than assumed: 63 to 68 percent of training groups in one study, with the composition rotating from all-wrong toward all-correct as model scale grows; and in another the exact-tie rate rises from 2.80 percent in epoch 1 to 7.73 in epoch 3 with the share at maximum reward rising from 64.6 to 85.2, so the reward saturates as the policy improves. Three families of remedy appear: reshaping the reward so a continuous signal does not collapse the group's relative spacing, reshaping the weighting so budget stops concentrating on solved prompts, and injecting a second signal active only where the scalar advantage is exactly zero -- privileged-context distillation, or a pairwise judge. The strongest evidence for the third is a restriction rather than an argument: distilling into zero-variance groups alone recovers 84.7 percent of the full gain. One source uses the phenomenon as a metric instead of a target, counting rescued and lost groups against a reference run because entropy and pass@k cannot distinguish exploration from degeneration. None of the remedies reduces how often groups collapse; they make an already-sampled group informative.
